title: Data structures in Python
summary: A second-year course on the core data structures of computer science, built in Python. Students compare lists and linked lists, then study stacks, queues, hash tables, binary search trees, heaps and graphs. Every structure is coded in full in class and analyzed for running time.
brief: Data structures in Python for second-year computer science students: 6 lessons of 75 minutes each, taught face to face in a classroom. Lesson 1, lists versus linked lists. Lesson 2, stacks and queues. Lesson 3, hash tables. Lesson 4, binary search trees. Lesson 5, heaps and priority queues. Lesson 6, graphs with breadth-first and depth-first search. The code demonstrated in class is written out in full. Grading: problem sets 40%, two quizzes 20%, final exam 40%.

segments.title: How a Python list is stored
segments.description:
Explain that a Python list is an array of references stored in one block of memory. Index lookup jumps straight to a slot, so it takes O(1).
Run the demo, then time `insert(0, x)` against `append(x)` on 100,000 items.
Before the timing runs, each student writes how many items must move to insert at the front of a list of 8 items, then checks with a partner.
segments.teacherNotes:
Answer: all 8 shift one place right; for n items, n moves, so O(n). Timings vary by machine; the gap, not the numbers, matters. Common mistake: thinking insert(0, x) is O(1) because it is one call.
`nums = [10, 20, 30, 40]`
`nums.append(50)`
`nums.insert(0, 5)`
`print(nums[2])`
`print(nums)`
`from timeit import timeit`
`big = list(range(100_000))`
`print(timeit(lambda: big.insert(0, 0), number=1000))`
`print(timeit(lambda: big.append(0), number=1000))`
shown: Insert at the front of a list of 8 items: how many items must move?

segments.title: Coding a singly linked list
segments.description:
Write `Node` and `LinkedList` live with `insert_front`, `to_list`, `search` and `delete`. Draw boxes and arrows on the board beside each method.
Before running the demo, students write on paper what the list holds after inserting 9, then 7, then 3 at the front.
Then walk through `search` and `delete`, stressing the head case in `delete`.
segments.teacherNotes:
Answer: 3, 7, 9, since each insert goes in front. Costs: insert_front O(1); search and delete O(n) in the worst case. Students often forget that delete must reconnect the previous node to the node after the target.
`class Node:`
`    def __init__(self, value, next=None):`
`        self.value = value`
`        self.next = next`
`class LinkedList:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.head = None`
`    def insert_front(self, value):`
`        self.head = Node(value, self.head)`
`    def to_list(self):`
`        out = []`
`        node = self.head`
`        while node is not None:`
`            out.append(node.value)`
`            node = node.next`
`        return out`
`    def search(self, value):`
`        node = self.head`
`        while node is not None:`
`            if node.value == value:`
`                return True`
`            node = node.next`
`        return False`
`    def delete(self, value):`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            return False`
`        if self.head.value == value:`
`            self.head = self.head.next`
`            return True`
`        node = self.head`
`        while node.next is not None:`
`            if node.next.value == value:`
`                node.next = node.next.next`
`                return True`
`            node = node.next`
`        return False`
`items = LinkedList()`
`for v in (9, 7, 3):`
`    items.insert_front(v)`
`print(items.to_list())`
`print(items.search(7))`
`items.delete(7)`
`print(items.to_list())`
shown: After insert_front(9), insert_front(7), insert_front(3): what does the list hold, from head to end?

segments.title: Why append is amortized constant time
segments.description:
Use a simplified model: a list has a fixed capacity, and when it is full, a new block of double the size is made and every item is copied over.
In pairs, students tally how many items are copied while appending 8 items one at a time, starting from capacity 1.
Then extend the count to 16 appends and show that the total copying stays below twice the number of appends: the copies form the sum 1 + 2 + 4 + …, which is less than twice its largest term. Each append also writes one new reference, so the total work is O(n) for n appends and the amortized cost per append is O(1).
segments.teacherNotes: Answer for 8 appends: copies happen when adding the 2nd, 3rd and 5th items, copying 1 + 2 + 4 = 7. For 16: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15. Real CPython grows by a smaller factor, but the argument still holds. Common mistake: calling one append O(1) worst case.
shown: Model: capacity starts at 1 and doubles when full.

keyIdeas: A Python list stores references in one block of memory, so reading by index is fast but inserting near the front means shifting every later item.
A singly linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a reference to the next node, so inserting at the front is cheap but search must walk the chain.
Lookup by position costs O(1) in a Python list and O(n) in a linked list; insertion and deletion at the front cost O(n) in a list and O(1) in a linked list.
Appending to a Python list is amortized O(1): an occasional costly copy into a bigger block is spread over many cheap appends.
Deleting from a linked list needs a special case for the head, or the first node can never be removed.

vocabulary.definition: One link in a linked list: it holds a value and a reference to the next node.
A chain of nodes in which each node points only to the next one.
The first node of a linked list; the list is reached through it.
A value that says where another object is stored; a node’s next field is one.
An array that grows by moving to a larger block of memory when it is full; a Python list works this way.
Visiting the items of a structure one after another, such as following next from the head.
Linear time: the work grows in proportion to the number n of items.
The average cost per operation over many operations is constant, even if a few single operations are costly.

study.overview: A Python list and a singly linked list can hold the same values, but they are built differently, so their operations cost different amounts. A list keeps references side by side in one block of memory. A linked list keeps separate nodes, each pointing to the next. Lookup by position is O(1) in a list and O(n) in a linked list. Insertion and deletion at the front are O(n) in a list and O(1) in a linked list. Appending to a Python list is amortized O(1). This guide goes through these ideas with code and small examples. Next time brings a graded quiz (Quizzes) on what the course has taught up to today, and the Problem sets assignment is due at the start of next time. For optional further reading, see Goodrich, Tamassia & Goldwasser, Data Structures and Algorithms in Python (2013).

points.heading: A Python list: fast lookup, costly front insertion
points.explanation:
A Python list is an array of references stored in one block of memory. To read `nums[2]`, Python works out the address of slot 2 from the start of the block and jumps straight there. The list’s length does not matter, so lookup by index is O(1).
The cost shows up when you insert near the front. Every later item must shift one slot to the right to make room. For n items that is n moves, so `nums.insert(0, x)` is O(n), even though it is only one call. Deleting from the front shifts items the other way and is also O(n).
Example:
`nums = [10, 20, 30, 40]`
`nums.insert(0, 5)`
`print(nums)`
The items 10, 20, 30 and 40 each move one slot right, and the output is [5, 10, 20, 30, 40]. With 1,000,000 numbers in the list, the same call moves 1,000,000 items.

points.heading: A singly linked list: cheap front insertion, search by walking
points.explanation:
A singly linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value and a reference to the next node. The list object keeps only a reference to the first node, the head. The last node’s `next` is `None`.
Here is the code, including front insertion and search:
`class Node:`
`    def __init__(self, value, next=None):`
`        self.value = value`
`        self.next = next`
`class LinkedList:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.head = None`
`    def insert_front(self, value):`
`        self.head = Node(value, self.head)`
`    def search(self, value):`
`        node = self.head`
`        while node is not None:`
`            if node.value == value:`
`                return True`
`            node = node.next`
`        return False`
Example: call `insert_front(9)`, then `insert_front(7)`, then `insert_front(3)`. Each new node points to the old head and then becomes the head, so the chain reads 3 → 7 → 9, from head to end. Nothing else moves, so `insert_front` is O(1) however long the chain is.
The price is that nodes are not side by side in memory. To find a value, or the item at a given position, you must walk from the head one link at a time. Here `search(9)` takes three steps, and `search(5)` walks the whole chain and returns `False`. Search, and lookup by position, are O(n).

points.heading: Deleting from a linked list: reconnect, and handle the head
points.explanation:
To delete a node, you do not remove it from memory by hand. You change one reference so the chain skips it. The node before the target must point to the node after the target. If you left a gap instead of reconnecting, the rest of the chain would be lost.
The head needs its own case. The loop in the code below looks at `node.next`, and no node points to the head. So the head can only be removed by moving `self.head` itself. Without that branch, the first node can never be removed.
`    def delete(self, value):`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            return False`
`        if self.head.value == value:`
`            self.head = self.head.next`
`            return True`
`        node = self.head`
`        while node.next is not None:`
`            if node.next.value == value:`
`                node.next = node.next.next`
`                return True`
`            node = node.next`
`        return False`
Example: take the chain 2 → 5 → 7 → 9. Deleting 5 sets the `next` of the node holding 2 to the node holding 7, giving 2 → 7 → 9. Deleting 2 next takes the head branch: `self.head` moves to the node holding 7, giving 7 → 9. The empty check at the top stops the method from reading `self.head.value` when `self.head` is `None`.
Deleting at the head is O(1). Deleting elsewhere is O(n) in the worst case, because you first have to find the node.

points.heading: Why appending to a Python list is amortized O(1)
points.explanation:
A Python list reserves spare room. Most appends just fill the next free slot, which is cheap. When the block is full, Python allocates a bigger block and copies every reference into it. That one append is expensive, so a single append is not O(1) in the worst case. But the expensive appends are rare, and their cost is spread over many cheap ones.
Use a simplified model: the capacity starts at 1 and doubles whenever the list is full. Appending 8 items one at a time triggers copies when the 2nd, 3rd and 5th items are added. They copy 1, 2 and 4 items, so 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 copies in total. For 16 appends the copies are 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15.
The pattern is that 1 + 2 + 4 + … is always less than twice its largest term. So the total copying stays below twice the number of appends. Each append also writes one new reference. The total work for n appends is O(n), and the amortized cost per append is O(1).
Real CPython grows the block by a smaller factor than 2, but the same argument still holds.

handouts.title: Find and fix the bug in delete
handouts.usedIn: Find and fix the bug in delete

blocks.text: This `delete` method belongs to the `LinkedList` class written earlier today, with the same `Node` class. It is meant to remove the first node that holds `value`, and to return `True` if it removed one and `False` if not. It has a bug.
The faulty method
Test it on paper
The list is the chain 5 → 2 → 8, with 5 as the head. Run `delete(5)` line by line on paper. Write what the method does and what goes wrong.

blocks.hint: Say what the chain looks like afterwards and what the method returns.

blocks.text: Fix it
Write a corrected `delete` method. Then compare it with your partner's fix.

blocks.hint: Write the whole method, with its indentation.

handouts.key:
1. Tracing `delete(5)`: node starts at the head, 5. The loop checks node 2's value, which does not equal 5, then advances node to 2. It checks node 8's value, which does not equal 5, then advances node to 8. Node 8's next reference is None, so the loop ends. The method returns False. The chain remains head → [5] → [2] → [8] → None. The method checks only the node after the current node, so it never checks the head's value. Common slip: assuming the loop checks the current node's value.

2. Corrected method:
`    def delete(self, value):`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            return False`
`        if self.head.value == value:`
`            self.head = self.head.next`
`            return True`
`        node = self.head`
`        while node.next is not None:`
`            if node.next.value == value:`
`                node.next = node.next.next`
`                return True`
`            node = node.next`
`        return False`

Look for an empty-list check, removal of a matching head, reconnection around a matching later node, and the correct Boolean return values. An equivalent method using current and previous references is also correct. With the corrected method, deleting 5 produces head → [2] → [8] → None and returns True. Common slips: omitting the empty-list check, changing only a local variable instead of the head, or failing to reconnect the previous node to the following node.

blocks.text: Work alone for two minutes. Suppose a program handles a collection of items in two phases. For each phase, write the better structure, a Python list or a singly linked list, and a reason of a few words.
Phase 1: 100,000 readings are added one at a time at the end, then looked up many times by position.
Phase 2: new items are added again and again at the front of a long collection.

handouts.key:
Phase 1: Python list. Appending is amortized O(1) per reading, and lookup by position is O(1). Adding 100,000 readings takes O(n) total work, where n = 100,000. Look for a reason that connects efficient appending and indexed lookup to this phase. Common slip: calling append O(1) in the worst case; an append that resizes the backing array takes O(n).

Phase 2: Singly linked list. Each front insertion takes O(1): create a node pointing to the old head and update the head. A Python list takes O(n) per front insertion because its existing references shift right. Look for the front-insertion cost as the reason. Common slip: treating a single call to insert as constant-time regardless of how many references move.

segments.title: Stacks on a list and on linked nodes
segments.description:
Name the pattern: last in, first out (LIFO). Write `Stack` on a Python list live with `push`, `pop`, `peek` and `is_empty`.
Before running the demo, students write the four printed values for the code on the screen, then check with a partner.
Put the `Node` class from last time on the screen again. Write `LinkedStack` with `push` and `pop` at the head, and draw boxes and arrows beside each method.
segments.teacherNotes:
Answer: 2, 8, 5, 4. List push costs amortized O(1), and list pop costs O(1). Linked stack push and pop both cost O(1). Mistake: using `insert(0, x)` and `pop(0)` on a list stack, which is O(n). Popping an empty stack should raise `IndexError`.
`class Stack:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.items = []`
`    def push(self, item):`
`        self.items.append(item)`
`    def pop(self):`
`        if not self.items:`
`            raise IndexError('pop from empty stack')`
`        return self.items.pop()`
`    def peek(self):`
`        return self.items[-1]`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return not self.items`
`s = Stack()`
`for v in (4, 8, 2):`
`    s.push(v)`
`print(s.pop())`
`print(s.pop())`
`s.push(5)`
`print(s.pop())`
`print(s.pop())`
`class Node:`
`    def __init__(self, value, next=None):`
`        self.value = value`
`        self.next = next`
`class LinkedStack:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.head = None`
`    def push(self, value):`
`        self.head = Node(value, self.head)`
`    def pop(self):`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            raise IndexError('pop from empty stack')`
`        value = self.head.value`
`        self.head = self.head.next`
`        return value`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return self.head is None`
shown: s = Stack(); push 4, push 8, push 2. Then: print(pop), print(pop), push 5, print(pop), print(pop). What is printed, in order?

segments.title: Checking balanced brackets with a stack
segments.description:
Explain the rule: push each opening bracket, and at each closing bracket pop and compare. The text is balanced only if every pop matches and the stack is empty at the end.
Write `is_balanced` live using `Stack`.
Students trace `{[()]}` on paper, writing the stack after each character, then trace `([)]`. Partners compare and say where the second one fails.
segments.teacherNotes:
Answers: `{[()]}` ends with an empty stack, so True. `([)]` fails at `)`, where the pop gives `[`, not `(`, so False. The mapping dictionary pairs each closer with its opener. Cost: one pass, O(n).
`def is_balanced(text):`
`    pairs = {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'}`
`    stack = Stack()`
`    for ch in text:`
`        if ch in '([{':`
`            stack.push(ch)`
`        elif ch in pairs:`
`            if stack.is_empty() or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:`
`                return False`
`    return stack.is_empty()`
`print(is_balanced('{[()]}'))`
`print(is_balanced('([)]'))`

segments.title: Find and fix the bug in the bracket checker
segments.description:
Show a faulty `is_balanced`. Each student tests it alone on paper with `((` and `())` and writes what goes wrong in each case.
Students write a fix, then compare it with a partner’s.
Hear two fixes and test one live.
segments.teacherNotes:
Bugs: `((` returns True because the final stack is never checked. `())` pops an empty stack and raises `IndexError`. Fix: test `is_empty()` before popping and return `stack.is_empty()`. Watch for students who fix only one of the two.
`def is_balanced_bad(text):`
`    pairs = {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'}`
`    stack = Stack()`
`    for ch in text:`
`        if ch in '([{':`
`            stack.push(ch)`
`        elif ch in pairs:`
`            if stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:`
`                return False`
`    return True`

segments.title: Queues on a list and on linked nodes
segments.description:
Name the pattern: first in, first out (FIFO). Write `ListQueue` with `enqueue` using `append` and `dequeue` using `pop(0)`.
Write `LinkedQueue` with a head and a tail reference, and draw the chain with both references labeled.
Before running the demo, students write what prints and what remains in the queue, then compare with a partner.
segments.teacherNotes:
Answer: a, b, c print, and d remains. Enqueue at the tail and dequeue at the head are both O(1). Mistake: forgetting to set `tail` to None when the last node leaves. `ListQueue.dequeue` is O(n) because `pop(0)` shifts items.
`class ListQueue:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.items = []`
`    def enqueue(self, item):`
`        self.items.append(item)`
`    def dequeue(self):`
`        if not self.items:`
`            raise IndexError('dequeue from empty queue')`
`        return self.items.pop(0)`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return not self.items`
`class LinkedQueue:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.head = None`
`        self.tail = None`
`    def enqueue(self, value):`
`        node = Node(value)`
`        if self.tail is None:`
`            self.head = node`
`        else:`
`            self.tail.next = node`
`        self.tail = node`
`    def dequeue(self):`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            raise IndexError('dequeue from empty queue')`
`        value = self.head.value`
`        self.head = self.head.next`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            self.tail = None`
`        return value`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return self.head is None`
`q = LinkedQueue()`
`for v in ('a', 'b', 'c'):`
`    q.enqueue(v)`
`print(q.dequeue())`
`q.enqueue('d')`
`print(q.dequeue())`
`print(q.dequeue())`
shown: q = LinkedQueue(); enqueue a, b, c. Then: print(dequeue), enqueue d, print(dequeue), print(dequeue). What is printed, and what is left in the queue?

keyIdeas: A stack is last in, first out (LIFO). Push and pop work at one end only, so list push costs amortized O(1) and list pop costs O(1), using the end. Both operations cost O(1) on linked nodes, using the head.
A queue is first in, first out (FIFO). Enqueue adds at the back and dequeue removes from the front.
A linked queue keeps a head and a tail reference, so both enqueue and dequeue cost O(1). A list queue that uses `pop(0)` shifts every remaining item, so dequeue costs O(n).

A stack checks balanced brackets: push each opener, pop at each closer and compare, and require an empty stack at the end.

vocabulary.definition: A collection where items are added and removed at one end only, so the most recently added item comes out first.
A collection where items are added at the back and removed from the front, so the oldest item comes out first.
Last in, first out: the order in which a stack gives items back.
First in, first out: the order in which a queue gives items back.
The stack operations: push adds an item on top, pop removes and returns the top item, and peek returns the top item without removing it.
The queue operations: enqueue adds an item at the back, and dequeue removes and returns the item at the front.
A reference to the last node of a linked queue, kept so that enqueue takes O(1) time without walking the chain.
A double-ended queue. In Python, `collections.deque` adds and removes at both ends in O(1), and `popleft` removes from the front.

study.overview: A stack and a queue are two ways of controlling the order in which items leave a collection. A stack returns the most recent item first. A queue returns the oldest item first. Both can be built on a Python list or on linked nodes, and the choice changes the running time. This guide covers both structures, how a stack checks brackets, and why `collections.deque` is the right tool for a queue. Optional further reading: Miller & Ranum, Problem Solving with Algorithms and Data Structures Using Python (2011).

points.heading: A stack is last in, first out
points.explanation:
A stack is last in, first out (LIFO). Push and pop work at one end only, so the item you pushed most recently is the first one popped. The Back button in a browser behaves this way.

On a Python list, use the end of the list. `append` is amortized O(1) and `pop()` is O(1):
`class Stack:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.items = []`
`    def push(self, item):`
`        self.items.append(item)`
`    def pop(self):`
`        if not self.items:`
`            raise IndexError('pop from empty stack')`
`        return self.items.pop()`
`    def peek(self):`
`        return self.items[-1]`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return not self.items`

Avoid `insert(0, x)` and `pop(0)` for a list stack. They shift every item and cost O(n).

On linked nodes, use the head. Both push and pop are O(1). The `Node` class is the one from last time:
`class Node:`
`    def __init__(self, value, next=None):`
`        self.value = value`
`        self.next = next`
`class LinkedStack:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.head = None`
`    def push(self, value):`
`        self.head = Node(value, self.head)`
`    def pop(self):`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            raise IndexError('pop from empty stack')`
`        value = self.head.value`
`        self.head = self.head.next`
`        return value`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return self.head is None`

Example: push 4, push 8, push 2. The first pop gives 2 and the second gives 8. Push 5, and the next pop gives 5. The last pop gives 4. Popping an empty stack raises `IndexError`.

points.heading: Checking balanced brackets with a stack
points.explanation:
A stack fits bracket checking because the most recent opener must be the first one closed. The rule has three parts:
1. Push each opening bracket.
2. At each closing bracket, pop and compare. The popped opener must be the partner of the closer.
3. When the text ends, the stack must be empty.

The dictionary `pairs` maps each closer to its opener. The function reads the text once, so it costs O(n):
`def is_balanced(text):`
`    pairs = {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'}`
`    stack = Stack()`
`    for ch in text:`
`        if ch in '([{':`
`            stack.push(ch)`
`        elif ch in pairs:`
`            if stack.is_empty() or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:`
`                return False`
`    return stack.is_empty()`

Example 1, `{[()]}`. The stack grows to `{`, then `{[`, then `{[(`. The `)` pops `(`, the `]` pops `[`, and the `}` pops `{`. The stack ends empty, so the result is True.

Example 2, `([)]`. The stack grows to `(`, then `([`. The `)` pops `[`, but its partner is `(`. The pair does not match, so the result is False at that character.

points.heading: Queues are first in, first out
points.explanation:
A queue is first in, first out (FIFO). Enqueue adds at the back and dequeue removes from the front. A ticket line works this way: if Ana, Ben, Cy and Dee join in that order, Ana is served first.

A list queue uses `append` to enqueue and `pop(0)` to dequeue. Every `pop(0)` shifts all the remaining items one place, so dequeue costs O(n):
`class ListQueue:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.items = []`
`    def enqueue(self, item):`
`        self.items.append(item)`
`    def dequeue(self):`
`        if not self.items:`
`            raise IndexError('dequeue from empty queue')`
`        return self.items.pop(0)`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return not self.items`

A linked queue keeps two references, `head` for the front and `tail` for the back. Enqueue works at the tail and dequeue works at the head, so both cost O(1):
`class LinkedQueue:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.head = None`
`        self.tail = None`
`    def enqueue(self, value):`
`        node = Node(value)`
`        if self.tail is None:`
`            self.head = node`
`        else:`
`            self.tail.next = node`
`        self.tail = node`
`    def dequeue(self):`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            raise IndexError('dequeue from empty queue')`
`        value = self.head.value`
`        self.head = self.head.next`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            self.tail = None`
`        return value`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return self.head is None`

Example: enqueue a, b, c. Dequeue prints a. Enqueue d. Two more dequeues print b and c. The queue is left holding only d.

points.heading: Why a deque suits a queue better than a list
points.explanation:
Python’s `collections.deque` gives O(1) `append` at the back and O(1) `popleft` at the front. A list gives O(1) `append` but O(n) `pop(0)`. For a queue, the removal at the front is the operation that matters, so the deque wins.

This demo times 1,000 removals from the front of each structure, with 100,000 items in each:
`from collections import deque`
`from timeit import timeit`
`big_list = list(range(100_000))`
`big_deque = deque(range(100_000))`
`print(timeit(lambda: big_list.pop(0), number=1000))`
`print(timeit(lambda: big_deque.popleft(), number=1000))`

Exact timings vary by machine. The size of the gap is what matters.

A deque used as a queue:
`jobs = deque()`
`jobs.append('report.pdf')`
`print(jobs.popleft())`

Here is a hypothetical case to show the scale. Suppose a print server must serve 50,000 jobs, oldest first. Using a list, each `pop(0)` shifts every job still waiting. Added up, that is about 1.25 billion item moves. Using a deque, each `popleft()` is one O(1) step.

handouts.title: Find and fix the bug in the bracket checker
handouts.usedIn: Find and fix the bug in the bracket checker

blocks.text: Work alone. The function below is meant to check that brackets in a text are balanced, but it has bugs. Test it on paper with the two inputs, then write a fix. You will compare your fix with a partner afterwards.
The Stack class it uses
The faulty checker
Test 1: trace `is_balanced_bad('((')` step by step. What does it return or raise, and why is that wrong?

blocks.hint: Write the stack after each character, then what happens at the end.

blocks.text: Test 2: trace `is_balanced_bad('())')` step by step. What does it return or raise, and why is that wrong?

blocks.hint: Write the stack after each character, then what happens at the end.

blocks.text: Fix: write a corrected version of the function that gives the right answer for both inputs and for `{[()]}` and `([)]`.

handouts.key:
Test 1: Bottom of the stack is shown on the left.
- Start: empty stack.
- After the opening bracket at position 1: (.
- After the opening bracket at position 2: ((.
- The loop ends and the function returns True. This is wrong because both opening brackets remain unmatched. The correct result is False.
Look for a trace that keeps both opening brackets on the stack and identifies the missing final empty-stack check. Common slip: assuming the function checks the remaining stack automatically.

Test 2:
- Start: empty stack.
- After (: stack contains (.
- After the closing bracket at position 2: the function pops (, which matches. The stack is empty.
- At the closing bracket at position 3: `stack.pop()` raises `IndexError` with the message 'pop from empty stack'. The function never reaches its final return.
- The correct result is False because the last closing bracket has no matching opening bracket.
Look for the empty-stack exception at the last character. Common slip: saying the function returns False, even though the exception occurs before the comparison can finish.

Fix:
`def is_balanced(text):`
`    pairs = {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'}`
`    stack = Stack()`
`    for ch in text:`
`        if ch in '([{':`
`            stack.push(ch)`
`        elif ch in pairs:`
`            if stack.is_empty() or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:`
`                return False`
`    return stack.is_empty()`

The corrected function returns False for ((, False for ()), True for {[()]}, and False for ([)].

For {[()]}, the stack after each character is: {, {[, {[(, {[, {, empty. Each closer matches the opener popped from the stack.

For ([)], the stack contains ( after the opening parenthesis and ([ after the opening square bracket. At ), the function pops [, which does not match (. It returns False immediately.

Accept an equivalent complete function, including one that keeps the name `is_balanced_bad`. Look for an empty-stack check before every pop, a comparison against the matching opener, and a final check that no opening brackets remain. Non-bracket characters should be ignored. Common slips: fixing only one bug, placing the empty-stack check after the pop, or returning from inside the loop before all characters have been processed.

t_08b92c2c433c.prompt: A collection holds 1,000,000 numbers. You must insert one new number at the very front. Which is cheaper: a Python list or a linked list? Write your answer and one reason.
followUps: What has to happen to the 1,000,000 numbers already stored in a Python list when the new number goes in at index 0?

t_b6385606c8c7.prompt: A classmate says: “Appending to a Python list is O(1), so one append can never be slow.” Do you agree?

t_b8fe729bdd60.prompt: Suppose a print server receives 50,000 jobs and always serves the oldest job first. Option A: a Python list, with `append` to add and `pop(0)` to remove. Option B: a `collections.deque`, with `append` to add and `popleft()` to remove. Which do you choose? Give one sentence with the cost of each removal.

t_34f2182dd655.prompt: A list-based `Stack` and a `LinkedStack` both give O(1) push and pop, though the list version is amortized O(1) for push. If you had to write a stack for a real Python program, which would you choose, and what would make you change your mind?
followUps: What does ‘amortized’ mean for `append` on a list, and does that occasional extra cost matter for a bracket checker?
Which version is easier to write correctly and to debug, and does that count as a real reason to choose it?

t_ac4776ae0498.prompt: A program repeatedly inserts a new value at the front of a collection containing n values. Which comparison correctly describes the cost of one insertion?

choices.text: Python list: O(n); singly linked list: O(1).
Python list: O(1); singly linked list: O(n).
Python list: O(n); singly linked list: O(n).
Python list: O(1); singly linked list: O(1).

t_ac4776ae0498.explanation: A Python list shifts n references. A singly linked list creates a node pointing to the old head and updates the head. “Python list: O(1); singly linked list: O(n).” reverses these costs. “Python list: O(n); singly linked list: O(n).” incorrectly assumes front insertion walks the chain. “Python list: O(1); singly linked list: O(1).” overlooks the list’s shifts.

t_55ce4309ed20.prompt:
A singly linked list uses this method:
`    def insert_front(self, value):`
`        self.head = Node(value, self.head)`
`Node(value, next)` creates a node holding the value and a reference to the next node. Starting with an empty list named `colors`, the program calls `colors.insert_front("red")`, then `colors.insert_front("blue")`, then `colors.insert_front("green")`. What values appear from head to end?

choices.text: red → blue → green
green → red → blue
blue → red → green
green → blue → red

t_55ce4309ed20.explanation: Each new node becomes the head and points to the previous head. The successive chains are red, blue → red, and green → blue → red. “red → blue → green” treats insertion as appending. “green → red → blue” puts the latest value first but reverses the existing chain. “blue → red → green” handles the second insertion correctly but appends the third value.

t_0f773294e7c7.prompt: Use a simplified array model whose capacity starts at 1 and doubles whenever it is full. A program appends 32 values. Resizing copies 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 existing references, and the appends write 32 new references. What does this show about append?

choices.text: Every append has O(1) worst-case cost.
The appends take O(n²) total work.
The appends have O(1) amortized cost.
Every append has O(n) copying cost.

t_0f773294e7c7.explanation: The total work is proportional to the number of appends: 31 copies plus 32 writes here. More generally, n appends take O(n) total work, giving O(1) amortized work per append. “Every append has O(1) worst-case cost.” ignores an append that triggers a large copy. “The appends take O(n²) total work.” incorrectly treats every append as copying the whole array. “Every append has O(n) copying cost.” overlooks appends that use spare capacity.

t_1bd70c58d887.prompt: For a collection of n values, reading the value at position n − 1 takes O(1) time in a Python list but O(n) time in a singly linked list that stores only a head reference.

choices.text: True
False

t_1bd70c58d887.explanation: A Python list accesses the slot directly by index. The linked list must follow next references from the head to the last node. That traversal grows with n.

t_f4e1126ad82b.prompt:
A singly linked list named `scores` contains 12 → 19 → 27. Each node has `value` and `next` attributes; the last node’s `next` is `None`. It uses this faulty method:
`    def delete(self, value):`
`        node = self.head`
`        while node.next is not None:`
`            if node.next.value == value:`
`                node.next = node.next.next`
`                return True`
`            node = node.next`
`        return False`
What does `scores.delete(12)` return, and what chain remains? Write the checks that must be added before `node = self.head` so deletion also handles an empty list and a matching head.
t_f4e1126ad82b.answer:
It returns False and leaves 12 → 19 → 27 unchanged. Add:
`        if self.head is None:`
`            return False`
`        if self.head.value == value:`
`            self.head = self.head.next`
`            return True`
t_f4e1126ad82b.explanation: The loop checks only the value in the next node, so it never checks 12 at the head. The empty-list check prevents accessing `node.next` when `node` is `None`. The head check removes the matching first node by moving the head reference to its successor. The existing loop then handles deletion after the head.

t_aef41794965a.prompt: A list-backed stack named history uses `append` for push and `pop()` for pop. It pushes 11, 6 and 19, pops once, pushes 7, and pops again. Which values do the two pops return, in order?

choices.text: 11, then 6
19, then 6
19, then 7
7, then 19

t_aef41794965a.explanation: The first pop removes 19, the most recently pushed value. Pushing 7 makes it the new top, so the second pop removes 7. “11, then 6” uses FIFO order. “19, then 6” overlooks the push of 7. “7, then 19” reverses the order of the two pops.

t_b85bea308c6a.prompt: A linked queue named requests has one node containing ‘scan’. Both `head` and `tail` reference that node. Its dequeue method saves the value and runs `self.head = self.head.next`. What must happen before the method returns the saved value?

choices.text: Keep `self.tail` pointing to the removed node.
Set `self.head = self.tail` to preserve the node.
Set `self.tail.next = self.head` to close the chain.
Set `self.tail = None` because the queue is empty.

t_b85bea308c6a.explanation: Removing the only node makes `head` equal to None. Setting `tail` to None keeps both references consistent with an empty queue. “Keep `self.tail` pointing to the removed node” leaves a stale tail reference. “Set `self.head = self.tail` to preserve the node” restores the removed node. “Set `self.tail.next = self.head` to close the chain” changes the removed node’s link but leaves the stale tail reference.

t_ea872ef42518.prompt: Suppose a help desk stores 12,000 requests and handles the oldest request first. Which implementation and removal cost best fit this queue?

choices.text: Use a list with `append` and `pop(0)`; removal costs O(1).
Use a deque with `append` and `popleft()`; removal costs O(1).
Use a list with `append` and `pop()`; removal costs O(1).
Use a deque with `append` and `popleft()`; removal costs O(n).

t_ea872ef42518.explanation: Appending at the back and removing from the front preserves FIFO order. A deque performs both operations in O(1). “Use a list with `append` and `pop(0)`; removal costs O(1)” gives the wrong cost: front removal shifts the remaining items and costs O(n). “Use a list with `append` and `pop()`; removal costs O(1)” removes the newest request. “Use a deque with `append` and `popleft()`; removal costs O(n)” assigns the list’s front-removal cost to a deque.

t_5b1ceb911ee7.prompt: A bracket checker that pushes openers, compares each closer with the popped opener, and checks for an empty stack at the end rejects `[{()}]` because different bracket types are nested.

choices.text: True
False

t_5b1ceb911ee7.explanation: Different bracket types can be nested. The openers enter the stack in the order [, {, (. The closers ), }, ] match them in reverse order. The stack ends empty, so the checker accepts the expression.

t_555f8c84d553.prompt:
This bracket checker uses the end of a Python list as a stack. `append` pushes, `pop()` removes the top, and `not pending` tests whether the stack is empty.
`def check_delimiters(text):`
`    matches = {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'}`
`    pending = []`
`    for symbol in text:`
`        if symbol in '([{':`
`            pending.append(symbol)`
`        elif symbol in matches:`
`            if pending.pop() != matches[symbol]:`
`                return False`
`    return True`
Explain what happens for the inputs `{` and `}}`. Then write the corrected condition inside the closing-bracket branch and the corrected final return line.
t_555f8c84d553.answer:
For `{`, the function returns True even though an opener remains. For `}}`, the first closer calls `pop()` on an empty list and raises IndexError. Replace the condition with:
`            if not pending or pending.pop() != matches[symbol]:`
Replace the final return line with:
`    return not pending`
t_555f8c84d553.explanation: The empty-stack test must come before the pop. Python’s `or` skips the pop when `not pending` is True, so an unmatched closer returns False without raising IndexError. The final empty-stack test rejects unmatched openers. Both corrections are needed.

t_179747c3c561.title: Problem sets: Python lists versus linked lists
t_179747c3c561.prompt: Write your own Python code and explanations. This assignment counts toward Problem sets (40% of the course grade). It is due at the start of next time. Your work is scored using the rubric below. Each criterion earns 1–4 points, for a total of 12 points.
steps:
Start with the complete code below. Add a method named `count(self, value)` to `LinkedList`. It must return the number of nodes whose value equals `value`, without changing the chain. Walk through the nodes using their next references. Do not convert the chain to a Python list.
`class Node:`
`    def __init__(self, value, next=None):`
`        self.value = value`
`        self.next = next`
`class LinkedList:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.head = None`
`    def insert_front(self, value):`
`        self.head = Node(value, self.head)`
`    def to_list(self):`
`        out = []`
`        node = self.head`
`        while node is not None:`
`            out.append(node.value)`
`            node = node.next`
`        return out`

Add a method named `remove_front(self)` to the same class. It must remove the head node and return `True` when the chain is nonempty. It must return `False` when the chain is empty. It must leave every remaining node in its original order. Write the whole method with its indentation.

Run the following demonstration after your class definitions. Record every printed line. Explain which reference changes during each successful removal. Then create an empty linked list named `empty_chain` and show that counting 14 returns 0 and removing its head returns `False`.
`inventory = LinkedList()`
`for value in (14, 22, 14, 35, 14):`
`    inventory.insert_front(value)`
`print(inventory.to_list())`
`print(inventory.count(14))`
`print(inventory.remove_front())`
`print(inventory.to_list())`
`print(inventory.count(14))`
`print(inventory.remove_front())`
`print(inventory.to_list())`

For a chain containing n nodes, give the running time of your counting method and your head-removal method. Explain each answer by naming the work the method performs. Compare head removal with removing the front item from an array-backed Python list containing n references. Explain why the Python list must shift references while your linked list does not.
t_179747c3c561.answerKey:
1. Add this method inside `LinkedList`:
`    def count(self, value):`
`        total = 0`
`        node = self.head`
`        while node is not None:`
`            if node.value == value:`
`                total += 1`
`            node = node.next`
`        return total`
The method visits every node and changes only local variables. The chain remains unchanged.
2. Add this method inside `LinkedList`:
`    def remove_front(self):`
`        if self.head is None:`
`            return False`
`        self.head = self.head.next`
`        return True`
The empty check prevents accessing an attribute of `None`. For a nonempty chain, moving the head reference removes the first node from the chain.
3. The printed lines, in order, are:
`[14, 35, 14, 22, 14]`
`3`
`True`
`[35, 14, 22, 14]`
`2`
`True`
`[14, 22, 14]`
The first removal changes the head reference from the first 14 node to the 35 node. The second changes it from the 35 node to the following 14 node. No remaining node’s next reference changes. An empty-chain check is:
`empty_chain = LinkedList()`
`print(empty_chain.count(14))`
`print(empty_chain.remove_front())`
Expected output:
`0`
`False`
4. Counting takes O(n) time because it visits all n nodes, including when no value matches. Head removal takes O(1) time because it checks the head and changes one reference, regardless of chain length. Removing the front item from an array-backed Python list takes O(n) time: the remaining n − 1 references shift left. A linked list changes its head reference and leaves the remaining nodes and their next references in place.

steps:
Compare a Python list with a singly linked list that stores only a head reference. Assume each contains n items.
(a) Give the running time for reading the item at position i in each structure, using worst-case time for the linked list.
(b) Give the running time for inserting a new item at the front of each structure. Explain why the costs differ. (5 points)

Complete the list-backed stack below by writing its entire push and pop methods. Push must add at the end of the list. Pop must remove and return the most recently pushed item. If the stack is empty, pop must raise IndexError. Then state the running time of each method, identifying any amortized cost.

`class TrayStack:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.items = []` (5 points)

Trace a stack-based bracket check on the expression `[r](s)`. The checker pushes each opening bracket. At each closing bracket, it rejects an empty stack; otherwise, it pops and compares with the matching opener. It ignores other characters and accepts only if the stack is empty at the end.
Write the stack after each bracket character, with the bottom on the left. Then state whether the expression is balanced and explain your answer. (3 points)

A list-backed queue contains `[14, 27, 39, 52]`, with the front on the left. Enqueue uses append, and dequeue uses pop(0).
(a) One dequeue occurs. Give the returned value, the remaining list and the number of remaining item references shifted toward the front.
(b) State the running time of dequeue for a queue containing n items with this implementation. State the running time of popleft on a collections.deque. (5 points)
t_4380c9f8752d.answerKey:
1. (a) Python list: O(1), because the position can be accessed directly. Singly linked list: O(n) in the worst case, because reaching the position requires following next references. Award 1 point for each correct cost.
(b) Python list: O(n). Singly linked list: O(1). Award 1 point for each correct cost. Award 1 point for explaining that the Python list shifts existing references, while the linked list links the new node to the old head and updates the head reference. (5 points)
2. Correct methods:
`    def push(self, item):`
`        self.items.append(item)`
`    def pop(self):`
`        if not self.items:`
`            raise IndexError('pop from empty stack')`
`        return self.items.pop()`
Award 1 point for a correctly defined push method that appends at the end; 1 point for checking emptiness and raising IndexError; 1 point for a correctly defined pop method that removes and returns the last item; 1 point for push costing amortized O(1); and 1 point for pop costing O(1). Equivalent correct code and other exception messages are acceptable. (5 points)
3. After [: ['[']. After ]: []. After (: ['(']. After ): []. The expression is balanced: both closing brackets match their popped openers, and the final stack is empty. Award 1 point for the first two stack states; 1 point for the last two stack states; and 1 point for the correct conclusion supported by matching pairs and an empty final stack. (3 points)
4. (a) The returned value is 14. The remaining list is [27, 39, 52]. Three references shift toward the front. Award 1 point for each answer.
(b) The list-backed dequeue costs O(n). A deque’s popleft costs O(1). Award 1 point for each correct cost. (5 points)

t_e16688fde904.title: Problem sets: Stacks and queues
t_e16688fde904.prompt: Write your own Python code and explanations. This assignment counts toward Problem sets (40% of the course grade). It is due at the start of next time. Each student’s work is done and scored alone. Your work is scored using the rubric below. Each criterion earns 1–4 points, for a total of 12 points.
steps:
Write `nesting_depth(text)`. It must return the greatest number of opening brackets waiting to be closed at any point in a balanced text. Return −1 if the brackets are unbalanced. Recognize parentheses, square brackets and braces, and ignore other characters. Return 0 for text without brackets. Use the complete stack below. Keep a counter for the current depth and another for the greatest depth reached. Check for an empty stack before popping, compare bracket types, and check for leftover openers at the end. Include the stack and your function together so they run in a fresh Python session. Explain how the counters change when an opener or a matching closer appears.
`class Stack:`
`    def __init__(self):`
`        self.items = []`
`    def push(self, item):`
`        self.items.append(item)`
`    def pop(self):`
`        if not self.items:`
`            raise IndexError('pop from empty stack')`
`        return self.items.pop()`
`    def is_empty(self):`
`        return not self.items`

Write `alternate_service(left, right)`. Its arguments are Python lists representing two queues, with the oldest item first. Return a new Python list of service order. Take one item from the left queue, then one from the right queue, and repeat. Once either queue is empty, continue serving the other in its original order. Do not change either input list. Include `from collections import deque` with your function. Use `deque(left)` and `deque(right)` to create separate queues containing the input items in their original order. A deque is false when empty and true otherwise, so `if queue:` and `while queue:` can test whether it contains items. Remove items with `popleft()` and add served items to the result with `append`. Explain why each queue preserves FIFO order.

Test both functions and explain the results. For `nesting_depth`, use `'{a[b(c)d]e}'`, `'x+y'`, `'(m]n'`, `'z}'` and `'{{p}'`. Record the return value for each input and explain the deepest nesting or the reason for rejection. For `alternate_service`, use `left = ['Lena', 'Omar', 'Pia']` and `right = ['Raj']`; then test an empty left list with `right = ['Sol', 'Tess']`, and finally two empty lists. Record the returned lists and confirm that the input lists keep their original contents. Explain the worst-case running time of each function. Use n for the length of the text and m for the total number of items in both queues. Include the cost of constructing the deques.
t_e16688fde904.answerKey:
1. Use the supplied Stack definition with this function. An opener increases the current depth; a matching closer decreases it. The greatest depth records the largest current depth reached. Reject a closer without an opener, a mismatched closer or leftover openers.
`def nesting_depth(text):`
`    pairs = {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'}`
`    stack = Stack()`
`    depth = 0`
`    greatest = 0`
`    for ch in text:`
`        if ch in '([{':`
`            stack.push(ch)`
`            depth += 1`
`            if depth > greatest:`
`                greatest = depth`
`        elif ch in pairs:`
`            if stack.is_empty() or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:`
`                return -1`
`            depth -= 1`
`    if not stack.is_empty():`
`        return -1`
`    return greatest`
2. Constructing separate deques preserves the input lists. Each removal takes the oldest remaining item from its queue. Testing each queue separately lets the remaining queue continue after the other becomes empty.
`from collections import deque`
`def alternate_service(left, right):`
`    left_queue = deque(left)`
`    right_queue = deque(right)`
`    served = []`
`    while left_queue or right_queue:`
`        if left_queue:`
`            served.append(left_queue.popleft())`
`        if right_queue:`
`            served.append(right_queue.popleft())`
`    return served`
3. For ‘{a[b(c)d]e}’, nesting_depth returns 3: the current depths after bracket characters are 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 0. For ‘x+y’, it returns 0 because there are no brackets. For ‘(m]n’, it returns −1 because ] does not match (. For ‘z}’, it returns −1 because } has no opener. For ‘{{p}’, it returns −1 because one { remains. The queue tests return [‘Lena’, ‘Raj’, ‘Omar’, ‘Pia’], [‘Sol’, ‘Tess’] and [], respectively. The original input lists remain unchanged because removals act on newly constructed deques. The bracket function has O(n) worst-case total time: it scans the text once, with amortized O(1) pushes and O(1) pops. Constructing both deques takes O(m); each of the m items is removed once in O(1) and appended to the result in amortized O(1). The queue function therefore takes O(m) total time.
